rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention and resolution pattern will guide window trimming and selectivity adjustments.

Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure how the critical pairs respond to slope.
The six-minute gradient retains full resolution, with the closest pair at R = 2.46. Test four minutes to further shorten the method while checking whether that pair remains above R = 1.5.

The four-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Test higher temperature at the same slope to shorten retention and determine whether temperature improves that pair’s selectivity before further acceleration.
Heating reduced the first pair’s resolution substantially. Test the lowest temperature at the same gradient to see whether cooling builds enough selectivity margin to permit a shorter gradient.

Cooling improved the critical pair to R = 2.48. Test a two-minute gradient with a narrower solvent window to limit compression, retaining the low temperature that favors separation; monitor the last peak for delayed elution during the final hold.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward by 0.05 while preserving gradient slope and the favorable low temperature. This should accelerate the late peak, which currently elutes during the hold, while testing whether the first pair retains full resolution.

The previous window shift shortened late elution without reducing the critical pair’s resolution. Shift upward one more grid step at unchanged slope to seek another faster method with maximum CRF, checking for compression of the earliest peaks.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while keeping the strong endpoint and low temperature. The narrower, shallower gradient may preserve critical-pair resolution while advancing the last peak; check whether the earliest peaks become insufficiently retained.

The current method has maximum CRF and a critical-pair resolution of 1.77. Raise temperature by one step to shorten late retention while testing whether that resolution margin accommodates the temperature-induced loss of selectivity.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic can shorten the method, returning to 25 C to favor critical-pair selectivity. This probes the early-retention boundary; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to phi0 = 0.30 to avoid the early-peak compression seen at 0.35. A slightly shallower gradient may offset the selectivity loss at 35 C, testing a warmer fully resolved method while monitoring late-peak retention during the hold.

Lower the starting organic fraction to retain the first pair more strongly, and return to 30 C, which previously preserved full resolution. This tests a short-gradient alternative with a shallower slope than injection 10, seeking additional resolution margin while maintaining maximum CRF.

Test one temperature step above the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, changing no other parameter. This directly checks whether faster late elution is possible at maximum CRF; if the first pair falls below 1.5, retain injection 10 as the preferred fast method.

The temperature boundary is now bracketed: 30 C resolves the first pair, whereas 35 C does not. Since maximum CRF is already secured, test a cooler, slightly shallower two-minute gradient for greater resolution margin with only a modest retention-time tradeoff.

Raise injection 15’s temperature one step to shorten late elution while retaining the slightly shallower gradient. This should provide a nearby maximum-CRF alternative; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 10 the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Test a cooler, narrower two-minute gradient to increase the first pair’s resolution margin while keeping it away from the unretained region; the strong final hold should still elute all six compounds promptly.

Raise injection 17’s temperature by one step to shorten the late peak’s hold-phase retention, using its R = 1.85 margin to accommodate some selectivity loss. Injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Raise injection 17’s endpoint to accelerate the late peak while retaining the temperature that favors first-pair selectivity. This tests an intermediate solvent window expected to preserve maximum CRF with more resolution margin than the warmer alternatives.

Maximum CRF is already achieved, and injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Test a four-minute gradient with the trimmed window to establish a short alternative with greater critical-pair resolution margin than the two-minute methods.

Raise the temperature of injection 20 to shorten retention while using its critical-pair resolution margin of 2.30. This tests a warmer, fully resolved alternative without changing gradient slope; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Back off one temperature step from injection 21’s marginal first-pair resolution to seek a larger separation margin while retaining a sub-five-minute last peak. Maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test one shallower endpoint step from injection 15 to seek additional critical-pair resolution margin within a two-minute gradient. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise injection 23’s temperature one step to accelerate the late peak while using its critical-pair resolution margin of 1.90. This tests another short maximum-CRF candidate; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

For the final injection, test a nearby two-minute method expected to retain full resolution, using lower starting organic to keep the early peaks well retained. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with its last peak at 2.58 minutes.
